channel.title: PC Workman — Build in Public Blog
channel.description: Three weekly series documenting the development of PC Workman, an AI-powered Windows system monitor: Monday Grind Blueprint, Wednesday Code Autopsy, Friday Shipped & Scarred. By Marcin Firmuga, HCK_Labs.

item.title: Forty-eight days, a taxi, and a game. Everything I have built has earned 70 zł.
item.description: 474 commits in 48 days of evenings after taxi shifts. What building a game alone actually cost, in hours, money and people, and what happens next.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #25: I Opened Google Search Console to Check Which of My Guides People Actually Find
item.description: Poland sends 33 clicks in six months. The Netherlands, where I scanned barcodes eighteen months ago, sends 32 and has the highest click rate on the list.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #25: I Do Not Have a Job. My CV Keeps Coming Back. I Am 22.
item.description: Fifteen months from a warehouse to a Microsoft Store app and a game at 0.4.0. Everything earned so far: 70 zł. Maybe building more was the wrong question.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #24: I Finished It Two Days Early, and I Did Not Choose a Single Thing That Is in It
item.description: A stranger found the game, played it and sent four things that were wrong. I gave him a date. Three with a date are finished. The one without has not moved.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #24: Someone Found My Game Through Google’s AI
item.description: A player found Scaling Laws through Google’s AI, played it and sent five things that were wrong, including an idea I had never written down: cancel anything.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #24: One Evening, a Pen and a Piece of Paper Found Four Things 1115 Tests Had Not
item.description: Samanta played Scaling Laws for one evening and took notes. A paragraph that never reached the game, music that stepped at the seam, and a test that caught my fix.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #23: Somebody Arrived on My Site With a Broken SSD and Left With a Game About Running an AI Lab
item.description: 23 troubleshooting guides written in summer. By autumn Google shows the site 200 times a day, and twenty people who came about a failing disk downloaded the game.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #23: Nothing in Your Build Fails When Your README Starts Lying
item.description: My README said a coasting company goes insolvent in three years. The harness says the fifth. How one unmeasured number lived for three weeks across three websites.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #23: Most Developers Have Never Seen Their Own Application
item.description: Six hours before release, Scaling Laws opened with its title bar off the screen and its bottom bar behind the taskbar. Why the editor could never show me that.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #22: On Wednesday I Wrote About Not Hearing Back. By Thursday Two More People Had Put My Name Forward.
item.description: Fourteen months of building did not get me a referral. Admitting I had been waiting did. Plus the tutorial bug my partner found by reading slower than every test.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #22: A Month Ago Three People I Have Never Met Passed My CV to a Company
item.description: A month after strangers passed my CV to a company, nothing came back. Writing that down, because I posted the thank you at the time.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #22: Most Developers Test Whether Their Code Works. Far Fewer Test Whether Anyone Can Reach It
item.description: A ten minute script found five unreachable features in a three-week-old game. This week it goes over the eighteen month old app on the Microsoft Store.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #21: Five Functions Came Back Unreachable. One Was an Entire Progression System.
item.description: The node promised curated corpora, took points, cash and four months, and delivered nothing. 526 tests passed because every test called the function directly.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #21: My Game Said a Training Run Would Take Eleven Days. It Took One.
item.description: Two formulas in Scaling Laws computed one training time and never compared notes. Pulling them into one function told the truth, and then broke the game.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #21: Twenty Weeks. Sixty Posts. Never Missed One. On Friday I Missed One.
item.description: Twenty weeks without missing a post, then a twelve-hour shift and an empty tank. Why the streak broke, and what Scaling Laws looked like fifteen days in.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #20: I Fixed the Same Bug Four Times. My Third Fix Was Part of the Bug.
item.description: Scaling Laws got a market with memory, and a save test that refused to go green: save in year four, load, play year five, end exactly like an uninterrupted run.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #20: I Booked Myself Seventy Hours of Taxi Shifts This Week
item.description: Before a week of seventy hours behind the wheel, one weekend to leave everything in a state where nothing was waiting on me. A release, a game on IndieDB and a CV.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #20: Five Months Ago One Command Deleted 130 Commits. On Friday I Was One Away From 1081
item.description: In March git push --force ate 130 commits. The recovery left my clone on the wrong branch for five months, 1081 commits behind, and git said all was fine.

item.title: The most dangerous bug does not crash. It succeeds.
item.description: Six real bugs that ran perfectly, passed every test and did nothing. A bare except that hid a NameError for four months, a Store shortcut that opened nothing, a scanner that accused the Print Spooler, and a claim in the article that was wrong until I checked it.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #19: Every Guide Says Finish What You Started. This Week I Started Two Games
item.description: In the month I could least afford distraction, I opened Unity. Scaling Laws is an AI company tycoon built on the real Chinchilla scaling law and 22 real accelerator generations.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #19: My Writing Landed on Spotify. A Post I Spent an Hour On Reached 14 People
item.description: HackerNoon turned my monolith article into audio the same week a post reached 14 readers. Sixteen new guides, an offline search, the biggest hck_GPT rebuild yet, and a script that quietly ate 38 commas.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #18: I Ship a Certified MSIX Package. In an Interview I Could Not Define a Package
item.description: Asked what a package is, I described the installer and never mentioned the answer I use every week: pip install, npm install. The hole between doing and explaining.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #18: Everyone Says Take the Leap. I Am Staying in Radom and Driving a Taxi
item.description: Every piece of advice says move to the big city and bet on yourself. This week I am doing the opposite, on purpose, because a bridge is not a leap.

item.title: Is My PC Healthy? A Five-Minute Check
item.description: Five checks that separate a normally busy PC from a real problem, without reducing system health to one synthetic score.

item.title: Why Is My RAM Usage So High?
item.description: Available memory and page faults explain more than a percentage alone. Learn when Windows memory use is normal and when to act.

item.title: What Is This Process in Task Manager?
item.description: File path, digital signature, parent process and behavior are stronger evidence than a process name by itself.

item.title: Will This CPU Work With My Motherboard?
item.description: Socket is only the first compatibility layer. Check generation, chipset, BIOS support and power delivery before buying.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #18: My First One-Star Review, and I Agreed With Every Word
item.description: A one-star review said the GUI needs refining and the learning curve is steep. I read it three times and agreed. The same week I shipped OVERCLOCK, Optimization Receipts and a roadmap to v2.1.0.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #17: Normally I Cut Open My Code Here. Today I Want to Talk About the Person Typing It
item.description: I am 22, I live in Radom, and I weld plastic in a repair shop. My nights belong to PC Workman. This week it reaches v1.8.5, and I still have not been given my first job in IT.

item.title: 6,533 Lines in One File: Breaking Up the Monolith Without Changing Its API
item.description: The hck_GPT response builder was split into eight mixins behind one facade. Two tests keep the files from growing back into a monolith.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #17: Opening One Menu Took 2 Seconds. It Now Takes 17 Milliseconds
item.description: Ten days of adding almost nothing, spent hunting the four places my own code had been lying to me. Plus Upgrade Readiness, which refused to wait for a calm week.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #17: My Tests Were Green. The App Was Broken. Both Were True
item.description: The engine week: a 6,533-line response layer split into seven modules, a refactor that silently switched the whole AI layer off, and a cleanup pass that sent every sidebar page back to the dashboard.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #16: My Assistant Is Not Allowed to Guess Whether That CPU Fits Your Board
item.description: Most AI assistants are trained to sound useful. Mine is not allowed to guess. One collector, shared hardware state, and four roadmap issues built from real power-user feedback.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #16: The Optimizer Could Freeze the Desktop. Then a Stranger Sent Me 50 PLN
item.description: On Monday my optimizer could freeze the Windows desktop. By Thursday a stranger with a 7950X3D and a flashed RTX 4090 had paid me and offered his PC as a test bench.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #16: An Optimizer's Most Important List Is Not What It May Touch
item.description: The scariest bug I caught all year, and I caught it on myself, on purpose. sleep_app was perfectly happy to freeze dwm.exe, explorer.exe, and PC Workman itself.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #15: I Spent the Weekend Trying to Break My Own App on Purpose
item.description: 100% CPU, 100% RAM, thermal throttling. It broke and froze my entire computer. Good. Better me than you. v1.8.2 ships the guard that makes it impossible.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #15: Sixteen Answers That Existed Only on Paper
item.description: My AI matched 16 questions with 100% confidence and returned nothing. The first week PC Workman was on the Microsoft Store, and the week a tester found the temperature pipeline broken.

item.title: From a Warehouse Floor to the Microsoft Store
item.description: A year ago I scanned barcodes and coded every night because I was afraid of disappearing. Today PC Workman — a Windows monitor with a fully offline AI — is on the Microsoft Store, permanently. The whole story, and the math underneath it.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #15: It Is Live on the Microsoft Store
item.description: A year ago that sentence was the last line of a roadmap I wrote but did not believe I would reach. 12 dead projects behind me, and a 2014 laptop that hits 94 degrees.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #14: Two Machines Rejected Me This Week. Neither Read a Line of My Code
item.description: Microsoft bounced the app over a blurry icon and a wrong link. Then LinkedIn shadowbanned the post about it because a filename looked like a suspicious link.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #14: Microsoft Store Said No — Over a Blurry Icon and the Wrong Link
item.description: My first .msix, a full Partner Center submission, v1.8.0 stable — and a rejection over a blurry tile icon and a privacy link pointing at my security policy. A checklist, not a no.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #14: My AI Had a Brain — It Just Couldn't Reach It
item.description: Two tested learning engines the chat never called — a bare except: pass swallowed the NameError that wired them in, dead for four months and silent.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #13: Every Gaming Tool Picks Your Overlay. Mine Starts Empty.
item.description: An in-game overlay that shows nothing until you choose, and greets you by the game you launched. v1.8.0 ships and the project turns one year old.

item.title: I Was Supposed to Fix Bugs. I Accidentally Built Two Features Instead. PC Workman 1.7.8
item.description: Thermal baseline learning and voltage SPC — the two features that grew out of a bug-fixing week. PC Workman 1.7.8.

item.title: I Built an AI-Powered PC Monitor in Python. 28 Strangers Shaped Its Brain. PC Workman 1.7.6
item.description: How 28 community members shaped hck_GPT's 82 intents. DeepMonitor, the 2.5D PC map and Wave 2 of the offline assistant.

item.title: Wednesday Code Autopsy #4: The Canvas Arc Nobody Uses — PC Workman
item.description: Tkinter's create_arc — the forgotten canvas primitive behind PC Workman's driver health gauge.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #3: I Built a Driver Booster Competitor From Scratch — PC Workman v1.7.2
item.description: The week's plan: driver health scanning without the bloatware — what became First Setup & Drivers.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #3: PC Workman 1.7.1 — The Foundation Great Release
item.description: Stats Engine v2 shipped: the SQLite time-series pipeline every later feature stands on.

item.title: Monday Grind Blueprint #2: 80 Processes Explained, 3 Issues Targeted, 1 Week to Ship
item.description: Growing the process library and committing publicly to three community-reported issues in one week.

item.title: Friday Shipped & Scarred #1: The Day git --force Deleted 130 PC Workman Commits
item.description: The week the repo died on a Tuesday. Recovery via reflog — 90 of 130 commits back — and the backup rule born from it.

item.title: Code Autopsy #1: How ~90 Lines Turned System Monitoring Into A Conversation
item.description: The first intent parser — the ~90-line seed that grew into hck_GPT's 82 offline intents.
